newsitem.title: UK: UK building society windfalls could fuel consumer boom.
newsitem.headline: UK building society windfalls could fuel consumer boom.

text.p: A flood of windfall payments from British building societies later this year could tip the already buoyant UK economy over the inflationary edge, economists said.

Britain's Woolwich Building Society announced on Monday that qualifying customers would each receive 450 free shares when it converts to a public company in July. That means the average member will receive 1,233 pounds ($2,090).
The Woolwich is only one of several building societies that will land fat payouts in the form of shares on the doormats of savers and borrowers this year.
Britain's largest mortgage lender, the Halifax Building Society, also plans to float around the middle of the year as do the Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock building societies.
On top of that, the Bristol and West Building Society will cough up 600 million pounds in cash to its members after it merges with the Bank of Ireland.

That adds up to a grand total of about 17 billion pounds flooding into millions of consumers' pockets later this year. "A decent chunk of that money is going to be spent," said David Fell, economist at Business Strategies Ltd.
Economists have repeated the mantra that economic theory states windfalls tend to be saved and Fell agreed that the bulk of the money would be ploughed back into savings.
But if even a quarter of the money is spent, about four billion pounds, that equates to about two pence off income tax.
"That will boost what is already decent consumer spending growth and if people spend a considerable portion of these windfalls, inflation will take off," Fell said.
He forecast consumer spending growth of about four percent in 1997 with headline inflation rising above three percent, from 2.7 percent year-on-year in December last year.
"But that is on the assumption that rates rise to seven percent or above." British base rates stand at six percent.

Much depends on how entrenched the feelgood factor is after elections due by May. But with the housing market recovering and tax cuts feeding through, there are few signs that consumers will put their wallets back under lock and key this year.
"Consumers remain buoyant and are prepared to take on more debt," said David Philpotts, economist at Schroders.
"With lower taxes coming, the housing market flourishing and any interest rate rises unlikely to be severe, there is little on the horizon to change that picture."

A one penny cut in the basic rate of income tax, announced in the November budget, will take effect in April. And the housing market is forecast to see price rises of around eight percent this year, following similar gains in 1996.

M0 money supply figures, released on Monday, suggested that high street tills have been ringing furiously. Annual M0 growth of 7.1 percent in December remains well above the government's zero-to-four percent monitoring range.
"Month by month changes don't correlate very well with retail sales but the fact that M0 remains buoyant suggests no sign of retrenchment on the consumer side," Philpotts said.
If the British consumer lets off steam after years of counting the pennies, Fell said it would be big-ticket items -- such as televisions, cars and holidays -- that would be bought.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is likely to come under pressure to raise interest rates well before any building society money becomes available.

"If the picture of strong sales is supported by the retail surveys from the CBI and the BRC over the next week, Clarke will come under heavy pressure to raise base rates in either January or February," said HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes.

The Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey is out on Friday. The British Retail Consortium's monthly sales monitor follows soon afterwards and Clarke meets with Bank of England Governor Eddie George for their monthly discussion of monetary policy next Wednesday. ($1.5899 Pound)
